newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - FOMC statement seen in limelight.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - FOMC statement seen in limelight.

text.p: Bond market players will have their magnifying glasses out on Tuesday to pore over the statement by Federal Reserve policy makers, assuming the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raises rates as expected.
The FOMC meets on Tuesday in Washington to decide the future course of monetary policy. The market is anticipating an increase of 25 basis points in the federal funds rate to 5.50 percent.
The statement, which usually accompanies any policy change, holds the key to the bond market's reaction, analysts said.

"If it's worded as a preemptive move or an insurance policy against a flare-up in inflation, the market will conclude its a one-time rate hike and we could see a rally," said Kathy Bostjancic, a money market analyst at UBS Securities Inc.

"But if it's worded to the effect that (the increase) is a move to get growth back towards its potential, or that we're moving away from neutral ... that could give the market the opinion there will be more increases going forward. That would put a more bearish tone in market psychology," she added.
Still, one Fed veteran said the tea leaves were not likely to yield any clear signals.

"They're not going to say it's the first of a series even if it is the first of a series," former Fed vice chairman Preston Martin told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV), referring to "Fedspeak," the careful and deliberate ambiguity of many Fed statements.
The FOMC usually announces its decision, if any, at 1415 EST/1915 GMT. Before the outcome is released, analysts see quiet, cautious trading.
If the Fed makes the expected move, experts see a short-term rally for the long bond, stemming from short-covering relief and a diminished inflation threat.
The crucial outcome should put a damper on the government's auction of $17.25 billion of two-year notes and pressure short-term notes early in the day.

MMS International Inc's Treasury Market Analyst, David Shabelman, said, "(Treasury is) going to have a harder time than usual selling those. There's not a lot of incentive to buy" because the sale's bidding deadline at 1300 EST/1800 GMT, will come before the end of the FOMC meeting.

If the Fed were to make no change in policy Tuesday, analysts do not expect a severe reaction from the bond market, with perhaps a temporary gain in short-term Treasuries and equities. But some said it might raise eyebrows about the credibility of the Fed.

"If the Fed says it believes in preemptive moves and then they do not move, people will be very confused ... Then what was all this talk about preemptive monetary policy?" asked William Dudley, Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc chief U.S. economist in an interview with RFTV.
Also due tomorrow are three economic barometers, but few are eyeing the data in light of the FOMC decision.
In the morning, March consumer confidence and weekly chain store sales are due.
At 1355 EST/1855 GMT, Redbook will release retail sales for the week ending March 22. The Redbook report will be released an hour earlier than usual so as not to coincide with any Fed's announcement.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted up 17/32 to yield 6.92 percent in late Monday trading.
